content: Tooth loss is defined as the premature loss of teeth. It is considered normal for deciduous teeth (commonly known as baby teeth) to be lost when they are replaced by permanent adult teeth. However, the loss of teeth outside this natural process is undesirable and typically results from injury or disease. Common causes include oral trauma, tooth injury, dental caries (tooth decay), and periodontal disease (gum disease). The condition of being without teeth or missing one or more teeth is referred to as edentulism. Differential Diagnosis of Causes of Tooth Loss The causes of tooth loss can be attributed to a variety of conditions, listed here in alphabetical order: Accidents or trauma Acromegaly Actalasia Chediak-Higashi Syndrome Chronic neutropenia Cholera Cyclic neutropenia Dentin dysplasia Diabetes Mellitus Down's Syndrome Drug-induced effects Hand-Schüller-Christian Syndrome Histiocytosis X Hypophosphatasia Hypophosphatemic vitamin D-resistant rickets Hypopituitarism Hypothyroidism Leptospirosis Lesch-Nyhan Syndrome Leukemia Localized tumors Lymphoma Odontodysplasia Osteomyelitis Papillon-Lefèvre Syndrome Periodontitis Primary hypothyroidism Psychosis Radiation exposure Reticulosis Syphilis Tuberculosis Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) Prevention of Tooth Loss Tooth loss caused by dental caries and periodontal disease can often be prevented through the maintenance of proper oral hygiene practices. This includes regular brushing and flossing, as well as routine dental check-ups, ideally twice per year. Additionally, the use of protective gear, such as mouthguards, football helmets, and goalie masks, can help prevent tooth loss due to trauma. Replacement of Missing Teeth There are three primary methods for replacing missing teeth: 1. Fixed dental bridges 2. Dentures 3. Dental implants
